name: Long-Term Digital Preservation
title: Long-Term Digital Preservation
answer: Long-term digital preservation is the set of policies, technologies and practices that keep research data and repository objects readable, usable and authentic for decades or longer. It covers more than backup: it addresses format obsolescence, media decay, software dependencies and the loss of contextual metadata. In research data and repositories, the scope includes datasets, code, documentation, derived files and the relationships among them. The goal is to ensure that a future researcher can find, open, understand and cite the preserved object without the original creator or system.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Long-term digital preservation is the set of policies, technologies and practices that keep research data and repository objects readable, usable and authentic for decades or longer. It covers more than backup: it addresses format obsolescence, media decay, software dependencies and the loss of contextual metadata. In research data and repositories, the scope includes datasets, code, documentation, derived files and the relationships among them. The goal is to ensure that a future researcher can find, open, understand and cite the preserved object without the original creator or system.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Preservation infrastructure typically combines redundant storage across at least two geographically separate locations with automated integrity checking. Storage may be on managed disk, tape or cloud object storage, but the key is that no single hardware failure or site loss destroys the only copy. Repositories often run fixity checks against stored checksums and keep multiple copies on different media or vendors. The infrastructure also includes a registry of file formats, software environments and persistent identifiers so that objects remain resolvable even when the original repository software changes.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done through a cycle of ingest, storage, monitoring and access. At ingest, a repository validates files, assigns persistent identifiers, extracts technical metadata and records the original checksums. Over time, staff or automated systems run fixity checks, watch for format obsolescence and plan migrations or emulation when a format or software stack becomes unreadable. Preservation actions are documented as events so that the object's history is transparent and repeatable. This is not a one-time export but an ongoing curatorial process.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk and provenance are handled through documented policies, deposit agreements and preservation metadata. A repository must record who created the data, who has rights to it, what access conditions apply and what changes have been made to the object over time. Provenance information, often captured in standards such as PREMIS, links each preservation action to the responsible agent and date. Risk management includes deciding which formats are acceptable, how many copies are enough and what to do when a rights holder withdraws permission or a file becomes corrupted. The repository's trustworthiness depends on being able to show this chain of custody to depositors and users.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Long-term digital preservation is moving toward more automated format identification, risk assessment and migration at scale. Machine learning is beginning to help classify file types, detect anomalies in large collections and predict which formats are most likely to become obsolete. Repositories are also exploring active preservation, where software environments are packaged with data so that future users can run old code without maintaining legacy hardware. The direction is less manual intervention and more continuous, policy-driven preservation across distributed networks of repositories.
